_raw_segments.segment: A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest.
He denied chest pain.
He denied dyspnea.
He denied palpitations.
He denied lightheadedness.
He denied diaphoresis.
He denied fever.
He denied lower-extremity edema.
He denied fatigue.
He worked in retail sales.
He had been lifting televisions in the preceding days.
His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg.
His initial vital signs included pulse of 100 beats/min.
His initial vital signs included temperature of 36.6 °C.
His initial vital signs included respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min.
His initial vital signs included oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry.
His initial vital signs included body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25.
He was directed to the local emergency department.
On physical examination, he was alert.
On physical examination, he was oriented.
On physical examination, he was in no acute distress.
Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border.
The point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced.
Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm.
Auscultation revealed normal first (S1) heart sounds.
Auscultation revealed soft second (S2) heart sounds.
A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1).
The murmur radiated throughout the precordium.
The murmur radiated into the abdomen.
The murmur radiated to the bilateral carotids.
The murmur was audible in the posterior thorax.
Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm.
Electrocardiogram showed moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy.
Electrocardiogram showed ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.
Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
